'''''Staphisagria macrosperma''''', formerly known as '''''Delphinium staphisagria''''', is a species of ''[[Staphisagria]]'' of the family [[Ranunculaceae]]. It used to belong to the [[subgenus]] or [[Section (botany)|section]] ''Staphisagria'' of the genus ''[[Delphinium]]'', but molecular evidence suggests ''Staphisagria'' should be a genus which is a [[sister group]] to the ''[[Aconitum]]''-''Delphinium'' clade.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last1=Jabbour|first1=Florian|last2=Renner|first2=Susanne|date=2011|title=Resurrection of the genus ''Staphisagria'' J. Hill, sister to all the other Delphinieae (Ranunculaceae)|journal=PhytoKeys|issue=7|pages=21–6|doi=10.3897/phytokeys.7.2010|issn=1314-2003|pmc=3261041|pmid=22287922 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jabbour|first1=Florian|last2=Renner|first2=Susanne S.|date=2012|title=A phylogeny of Delphinieae (Ranunculaceae) shows that ''Aconitum'' is nested within ''Delphinium'' and that Late Miocene transitions to long life cycles in the Himalayas and Southwest China coincide with bursts in diversification|journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution|language=en|volume=62|issue=3|pages=928–942|doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2011.12.005|pmid=22182994}}</ref> It is described botanically as a stoutly-stemmed, hairy biennial with large palmate leaves up to 6 inches (15 cm) across. The flowers are mauve-blue to blue, short-spurred, and up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) across, occurring in racemes. The plant grows to a height of 4–5 feet. It grows throughout the Mediterranean.<ref>D. Bown (2001), ''The Herb Society of America New Encyclopedia of Herbs and Their Uses'' p.192, London: DK.</ref><ref>Further details of its distribution may be found at: http://www.ars-grin.gov/~sbmljw/cgi-bin/taxon.pl?13475 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924160830/http://www.ars-grin.gov/~sbmljw/cgi-bin/taxon.pl?13475 |date=2015-09-24 }}</ref> All parts of this plant are highly toxic and should not be ingested in any quantity.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=''Delphinium staphisagria'' L., stavesacre|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Delphinium+staphisagria|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-09-24|website=PFAF Plant Database}}</ref>

== Names ==
The genus name ''Staphisagria'' and the common name '''stavesacre''' come from the [[Ancient Greek]] name mentioned by Dioscorides, σταφὶς ἀγρία (''staphis agria'', "wild raisin").<ref name=":1">{{cite book|author=Dioscorides|first=Pedanius|title=De materia medica|publisher=Ibidis Press|year=2000|isbn=0-620-23435-0|editor-last=Osbaldeston|editor-first=Tess Anne|location=Johannesburg|pages=708–711|chapter=4-156. Staphisagria}}</ref> Dioscorides described the plant as having wild grape vine-like leaves, but Barton and Castle considered the name as an allusion to the large wrinkled brown seeds.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Barton|first1=B.H.|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/74168#page/363/mode/1up|title=The British ''Flora Medica'', or, History of the Medicinal Plants of Great Britain|last2=Castle|first2=T.|publisher=E. Cox|year=1838|isbn=|volume=2|location=London|page=321}}</ref> This name derivation by Barton and Castle seems to have been arrived at independently by a modern horticulturalist, David Bassett, who also gives a detailed account of his experiences in growing this species.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Growing ''Delphinium staphisagria''|url=http://www.david.bassett.care4free.net/topics4/staphisagria.htm|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2012-05-10|website=www.david.bassett.care4free.net}}</ref>

Ancient Greeks also called the plant φθειροκτόνον (''phthiroctonon'', "louse killer") because of its use in traditional medicine to kill lice.<ref name=":1" /> This meaning is retained in many of the plant's common names in different languages,<ref name=":0" /> such as '''lice-bane''' in [[English language|English]], ''matapiojos'' in [[Spanish language|Spanish]], ''bit otu'' in [[Turkish language|Turkish]].

==History==
The use of herbal preparations made from ''S. macrosperma'' (''D. staphisagria'') seeds for destroying body-lice has been recognized since antiquity. The Greek physician [[Dioscorides]] and the Roman historian [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]] are most often mentioned in this context,<ref name=":0" /><ref name = Grieve>{{Cite web|url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/s/stavas90.html|title = A Modern Herbal | Stavesacre}}</ref> and in assessing this classical literature, Barton and Castle expressed the opinion that Dioscorides's description of ''staphis agria'' was consistent in most respects with the plant they knew as ''Delphinium staphisagria''.<ref name=":0" /> One of the founders of American [[pharmacognosy]], [[John Uri Lloyd]], writing in his famous ''Pharmacopeia'', also cited references to the use of ''D. staphisagria'' preparations in the writings of [[Nicander]] and [[Pietro de' Crescenzi|Crescenzi]]o.<ref>J. U. Lloyd (1911), ''History of the Vegetable Drugs of the ''Pharmacopeia'' of the United States'', Cincinnati.</ref>

Stavesacre is mentioned in a fourth century "[[Greek Magical Papyri|magical]]" [[papyrus]] codex from Egypt where it is said to have facilitated a man gaining an [[erection]]. The plant was to be crushed and mixed with water, then sprinkled around the house. However, the interpretation of the formula remains uncertain.<ref>William Brashear and Roy Kotansky, "A new magical formula" in ''Magic and ritual in the ancient world'', eds. Paul Allan Mirecki and Marvin W. Meyer (Leiden; Boston: Brill, 2002), 3-24.</ref>

A ''Delphinium'' preparation of some sort (most likely from ''D. staphisagria'') was apparently a standard issue to British troops at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] in 1815.<ref>F. Mitton and V. Mitton (1976). ''Mitton's Practical Modern Herbal'', p.102, London: W. Foulsham & Co. Ltd.</ref>

==Traditional uses==
As noted above, preparations made from ''S. macrosperma'' (apparently principally from the seeds) were used as a [[pediculicide]] throughout the last two millennia. [[Maud Grieve]], in her famous Herbal, written in 1931, refers to ''stavesacre'' as being a "[[vermifuge]]" and "vermin-destroying", as well as to its parasiticidal properties. She also mentions that it is "violently emetic and cathartic".<ref name = Grieve/><ref>M.Grieve (1931), ''A Modern Herbal.''</ref>

==Chemical studies==
Not surprisingly, in view of the long and well-known uses of stavesacre against insect and animal pests, ''S. macrosperma'' (''D. staphisagria'') was investigated by chemists as early as the beginning of the 19th Century. Two French scientists, [[Jean Louis Lassaigne|Lassaigne]] and Feneulle, were the first to isolate an alkaloid, called [[delphinine]] from ''D. staphisagria'' seeds in 1819.<ref>J. L. Lassaigne and H. Feneulle (1819) ''Ann. Chim. Phys.'' '''12''' 358.</ref> The completely correct molecular structure of delphinine was not determined until 1971,<ref>K. B. Birnbaum, K. Wiesner, E. W. K. Jay and L. Jay (1971) ''Tetrahedron Lett.'' 867.</ref> due to the chemical complexity of this substance, coupled with the technical limitations of the times. However, it was established quite early that delphinine was a member of the [[diterpenoid]] family of [[alkaloid]]s, and it is often cited in handbooks of poisonous plants as being a representative toxin of the genus ''Delphinium''. The occurrence of delphinine is somewhat limited in this genus. Although delphinine is the major alkaloidal constituent of ''D. staphisagria'' seeds, several other related diterpenoid alkaloids have been isolated from them as well.<ref>S.A. Ross, H. K. Desai and S. W. Pelletier (1987) ''Heterocycles'' '''26''' 2895-2904.</ref>
